title: tat tvam asi
tomorrow: a face from years ago, older now. how is it the same person?

segments.voice: Yesterday in tat tvam asi, the rivers: from the sea, to the sea, with Paul's one blood beside them. Today the whole week comes back, and so does the son's request.

The fifth but why in a row, from a kid in the back seat. It's hard not to sigh. Teach me more, sir, Shvetaketu says, again and again. And his father never says, I already told you. He says: so be it, my dear. Then he finds another picture.
screen: `THE FIFTH 'BUT WHY?'` → `TEACH ME MORE, SIR.` → `SO BE IT, MY DEAR.`

segments.voice: Listen to how the refrain climbs. That which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self. That is the real. That is the self. That you are. So that isn't pointing somewhere vague. The father has named it in the same breath: the finest essence, the real, the self. And each time his son asks again, he climbs the same stairs with a new picture. Now the week, in one breath. Vamadeva said I was Manu, and the sun, even now. A father promised the unheard made heard, and held up clay. Being alone wished to be many, and the Taittiriya's other view got its say. A sleeper went home like a bird to its post. Many trees made one honey, and the tiger stayed a tiger. Rivers from east and west came from one sea, and Paul spoke of one blood. Under each picture, the same request: teach me more. In the Chandogya, asking again isn't the lesson failing. It's how the lesson goes on.
screen: `THE FINEST ESSENCE, THE REAL, THE SELF.` · `A WEEK OF PICTURES.` · `CLAY, A BIRD, HONEY, RIVERS.` · then, large: `ASKING AGAIN IS HOW IT GOES ON.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly for a minute, across a room or down a hallway. Each time attention wanders, bring it back to your feet without scolding, the way the father answers: so be it, my dear. Then sit, and let the breath carry the rest.
Tat tvam asi: that you are, where that is the finest essence, the real, the self. The week's word, still climbing.
For keeps: tat tvam asi, and asking again is part of the lesson. That's the week.

screen: `DAY 1757 COUNTS.` → `TAT TVAM ASI · 6 OF 9.` → `TOMORROW: OLDER NOW. HOW IS IT THE SAME PERSON?`

howItsDone: In traditional study a student may ask a teacher to explain a passage again and again, and Chandogya 6, where the son keeps asking and the father keeps answering, is read as a model of that patience.

fork.setup: a friend reads 'that you are' and says 'that' is too vague to mean anything. what does the refrain point to?
options: the finest essence, the real, the self, named in the same breath.
a far-off heaven that the text never describes at all.
whatever each reader happens to want it to mean.
fork.reveal: the refrain names it first: the finest essence, the self of this whole world, the real, the self. only then: that you are.

original.note: Sanskrit: anima, the finest essence the refrain names before 'that you are'.

chat.meaning: In the Chandogya the son keeps asking, and the father answers 'so be it, my dear' with a fresh picture each time.

Shvetaketu.meaning: the son who keeps asking: teach me more

Vamadeva.meaning: the seer who said: I was Manu, and the sun

Taittiriya.meaning: an Upanishad that says non-being came first

Chandogya.meaning: the Upanishad where tat tvam asi is taught

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (that which is the finest essence, this whole world has that as its self; that is the real, that is the self, that you are, Shvetaketu; 'teach me more, sir'; 'so be it, my dear')
Chandogya Upanishad 6.9–6.13 (the bees and honey, the rivers and the sea, the tree, the banyan seed, the salt in water; each closes with the refrain and the son's request)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.10; Chandogya Upanishad 6.1–6.2; Taittiriya Upanishad 2.7.1; Acts 17:26 (the week's look-back)

notes: Block 'tat tvam asi', day 6 of 9 (1752–1760); also the week's last day (1751–1757), so the teach looks back over 1751–1756.

'Teach me more, sir' and 'so be it, my dear' paraphrase bhuya eva ma bhagavan vijnapayatv iti / tatha somya. Confirm the wording. The 'stairs' are the lesson's own image for the order of the refrain, not the text's. Schools differ on how far to take 'that points back to the finest essence' (the next days give Advaita, Ramanuja and Madhva).
